title: Fiqh close
hook: many schools, many scholars, one book, one sunnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spirit of the law, and your line: the aim behind it. Life, mind, faith, family, property. Did one rule show you what it was guarding? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

A shelf, to start. On it sits one Qur'an and a few volumes of hadith. Beside it stands a whole wall. Hanafi books, Maliki books, Shafi'i and Hanbali books, Ja'fari books, Zaydi and Ibadi books. Commentaries on commentaries. Rulings on wedding gifts, on contracts, on donkeys carrying too much, on hospital beds. For weeks now this path has walked along that wall, one school and one question at a time. Today is the end of the walk. So one last question before we leave the library: how does one small shelf turn into a wall, and still face the same way?
screen: `ONE SMALL SHELF.` → `ONE LONG WALL.` → `STILL FACING THE SAME WAY?`

segments.voice: Start with the word we've used all along. Fiqh means understanding. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives that person understanding in the religion. The verb there comes from the same root as fiqh. So the whole wall is, at heart, people trying to understand. Next, the roads. The jurists walked from the same starting point: the Qur'an first, the sunnah second. Then they reasoned out from there. Some leaned on the agreement of scholars, some on analogy, some on reason itself, as Ja'fari jurists do, some on the common good or the custom of a place. Different tools, different roads. Then, the difference. The Qur'an gives a direction for disputes: "if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger." The schools all claim that same reference point. And Bukhari records a hadith that explains their patience with each other: a judge who strives and gets it right has two rewards, and a judge who strives and gets it wrong still has one. Effort in good faith is honored even when it misses. Last, the direction. Stand at the back of a mosque at prayer time. One person folds the hands high, another lets them hang. One says amin aloud, another under the breath. Every row still faces the same point. That's the picture this block leaves behind. Many roads. One direction.
screen: `FIQH MEANS UNDERSTANDING.` · `ONE START, MANY ROADS.` · `TWO REWARDS, OR ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ROW FACES ONE POINT.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank the scholars. Bring one name to mind. It might be from these weeks: Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ja'far al-Sadiq. Or it might be closer: a teacher, an imam, a grandmother who knew how to pray and showed you. Somebody did the slow work of understanding so that someone else could stand in a row. Hold that person for a moment. If you pray, you may know the custom of asking Allah's mercy for a scholar when the name comes up; you can do that now. If you don't, simply say thank you, in your own head. The bell holds the time.
Fiqh close. The end of the block on fiqh, the understanding of the law: one book, one sunnah, many schools working from them. Today's word.

Your line: many roads, one direction. Today, when someone does a thing differently from you, look for where they're both facing. Tomorrow a new block starts: belief. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims follow the rulings of a school of law or a trusted scholar, and when a jurist's name is mentioned a Muslim may add a phrase asking Allah's mercy for them.

fork.setup: two jurists, both careful and sincere, reach different answers on the same question. what does the hadith say about them?

fork.reveal: the hadith in Bukhari honors the effort itself: two rewards for getting it right, one for striving and missing.

original.note: Arabic: understanding; the name for the study of Islamic law.

trapdoor: what you thought: fiqh is a rulebook handed down whole.
what it means: fiqh is understanding, the work of scholars drawing rulings from the Qur'an and the sunnah by many methods.
what a scholar hears: the hadith that Allah gives understanding in religion to those He wants good for, and the rewards promised to the striving judge.
recall: an answer to a question about the law
